title: Neural and Behavioral Perturbations via Optogenetic Inhibition of the Posterior Parietal Cortex during Motor Planning.
abstract: Deciphering neural mechanisms underlying neurostimulation is essential for developing targeted neurorehabilitation strategies, yet understanding the neural perturbations to behavior-related neural activity remains an area of active exploration. This study investigates the use of optogenetic inhibition to perturb motor activity and understand modulations to task-related neural activity in the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of non-human primates (NHPs). Multiple regions of the PPC near the interparietal sulcus (IPS) were transfected with the inhibitory opsin JAWS. Inhibition was applied during a center-out reaching task, leveraging a large-scale optogenetic interface that allowed for simultaneously monitoring of local field potentials (LFPs) during optical stimulation. Optogenetic inhibition induced significant behavioral effects, including prolonged reach times. Analysis of task-related neural features during the motor planning period revealed significantly increased theta power, theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC), and trends of increased coherence near the IPS and in the 7a/7b regions of the PPC. Optogenetic inhibition resulted in distinct perturbations to task-related neural activity including increased theta and gamma power, decreased gamma coherence, and diminished theta-gamma PAC in opsin-expressing regions, with minimal effects in opsin-deficient regions. These findings highlight that optogenetic inhibition induces local network decoupling of task-related neural activity. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the potential of this large-scale optogenetic interface to unravel the neural mechanisms underlying neurostimulation and its impact on task-relevant brain dynamics.Clinical Relevance-This work provides insight into how targeted optogenetic inhibition may be used to ameliorate pathological brain activity related to neurological disorders.
